column3: It joins a mistaken claim of good, requital on the Day, and divine knowledge of deeds, clarifying the focus's final warning.

The night-and-day signs do not materially clarify distortion of signs, judgment, or divine scrutiny already in view.

The call for humble, private prayer without transgression offers only a broad ethical opposite to deviation.

It describes the Quran as guidance and healing for believers but deafness and blindness for unbelievers, clarifying the divergent reception behind the focus.
It makes each person's good or evil deed return upon that person and denies injustice by God, directly grounding the focus's command to act.
It portrays denial of the Hour together with presumption about eventual good, a specific false-security contrast to arriving safe on that Day.
It warns against denying God's signs and turning away from them after the Book's clear proof has arrived.
Those who deny God's signs and are arrogant about them are assigned to the Fire, closely matching the focus's final contrast.
It states that the arrogant are turned from God's signs and, even when seeing every sign, do not believe, directly characterizing the focus's deviators.
It declares vain the deeds of those who deny God's signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, directly linking sign-denial to requital.
A veil between the Quran's recitation and those who disbelieve in the Hereafter helps explain their failure to receive its signs.
It calls no one more unjust than one reminded of God's signs who turns away and forgets prior deeds, closely uniting rejection and accountability.
It answers that God's signs came but were forgotten, so the rejecter is forgotten on the Day, directly anticipating the focus's final Day warning.
It recalls that God's signs were recited but the hearers turned back on their heels, a close portrayal of refusal of revelation.
It confronts deniers over rejecting God's signs without comprehending them, directly exposing an illegitimate response to the signs.
It joins disbelief in God's signs and the meeting with Him to loss of hope and painful punishment.
It depicts one who hears God's signs recited yet turns away arrogantly as though he had not heard them, directly parallel to the focus.
It calls the one reminded of God's signs who then turns away among the greatest wrongdoers and promises retribution.
It contrasts those striving to frustrate God's signs with those who believe and do good, supplying the focus's opposed moral paths.
It condemns one who lies about God and denies the truth when it comes, framing the false handling of revelation that the focus rebukes.
It censures disputing God's signs without authority, a close rhetorical analogue to slanting them.
It recalls that God's signs were recited, but the hearers became arrogant and criminal, directly leading into their final humiliation.
It records unbelievers calling the clear signs obvious magic when recited, a concrete case of refusing their evidentiary force.
